articles.title_orig: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mum and daughter
articles.title_zh: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mum and daughter
articles.content_orig:
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image)
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

articles.title_orig: John Kerry: America Must Now Follow China’s Lead on Clean Energy
articles.title_zh: John Kerry: America Must Now Follow China’s Lead on Clean Energy
articles.content_orig:
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.
“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.
after newsletter promotion
“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures rise as Nvidia stock recovers, 10-year yield nears 5%
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock rose premarket on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.
Shares had closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy . They fell 4.3% Monday.
Shares were 5.3% higher in premarket trading as of 5:47 a.m. ET.
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.
Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.
Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.
In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings.
In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.
Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said.
"It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.

articles.title_zh: US to seek Putin’s ‘blessing’ for Europe to join Ukraine talks
articles.content_orig:
ABU DHABI — U.S. officials will head to Moscow in person on Thursday to ask Russia’s Vladimir Putin to give his “blessing” to allowing European representatives to join future peace talks for Ukraine.
Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law who has been mediating talks in Abu Dhabi, told reporters he and White House envoy Steve Witkoff will head to Moscow to meet the Russian leader. They aim to agree a date for the next round of negotiations and to secure Putin’s approval for Europe to get a seat at the table.
“We need to have the Europeans at the table,” Kushner said, answering a question from POLITICO. “We have relayed to President Putin directly several times and to his team that the only way to get this done is to have them by our side and I think they are receptive to it.
“I believe that hopefully tomorrow in Moscow, Steve and I will be successful and President Putin will give the blessing for that to occur. I think that if he agrees to that we will be able to make a lot more progress on the issues that matter.”
Kushner also announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to what is likely to be “the biggest” exchange of prisoners since the start of the war. Numbers are set to be confirmed on Thursday, he added.
Kushner said that, overall, the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi were “substantive” and “tough.”

Nvidia stock closed down 5.47% on Tuesday amid the scandal over CEO Jensen Huang's affair, with earnings due on Nov. 17
Nvidia $NVDA stock was up 5.3% in premarket trading on Wednesday as of 5:47 a.m. ET, bouncing back from two straight sessions of losses amid the scandal over CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
Morgan Stanley $MS removed Nvidia from its list of top picks on Wednesday, according to CNBC . Nvidia stock had lost more than a quarter of its value since the bank first included it on Oct. 2. Analysts at the bank said in a note that Huang's leadership is "crucial" to where Nvidia is steering its strategy.
Nvidia stock ended Tuesday’s session 5.5% lower, with fresh reporting shedding light on the affair’s toll on the company.
Huang came back to work in person on Monday and sought to convey "business as usual," according to CNBC. He held meetings at the office on Tuesday, ahead of the company's earnings report on Nov. 17.
John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks, attributed the selloff to worries over possible new U.S. curbs and the chance that additional troubles could surface while the story unfolds, according to CNBC. "What else has Jensen done?" he said.
"It's not good for Nvidia . It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.
On Tuesday, Nvidia retained law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the independent investigation its board announced Sunday. Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, will lead the work, and a panel of independent directors will supervise it. The board said on Sunday that nothing it has seen suggests Nvidia 's trade secrets or U.S. national security were put at risk.
Huang apologized to employees in a message on Sunday. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote. The woman, Alice Huang, is not related to him and is suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of spying for China. China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the allegation unsubstantiated.
The Justice Department is conducting a criminal probe of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm suspected of illegally funneling Nvidia AI chips to China. Rosen Law Firm has filed a shareholder class action against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose, California. Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock extended its decline Tuesday, falling roughly 5% after dropping 4% in the prior session. Scrutiny centers on Alice Huang, whom the US government reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, and her ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dating back to at least 2023.
The Information reported that their rapport could have helped facilitate the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies, according to two people who know her and corporate records.
On Monday, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Congress needs more answers about the matter, adding that there are "real ⁠concerns that need to be addressed with respect to the ​Nvidia situation."

"We'll look into it," said Trump. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape."
The broader semiconductor sector wavered on Tuesday amid a broader market sell-off after a hotter-than-expected October inflation reading, which strengthened expectations for a rate hike next month.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ), which manufactures Nvidia chips, wavered, while semiconductor equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) slipped into red territory.

articles.title_orig: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt objects at Biden outside Irish university
articles.title_zh: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt objects at Biden outside Irish university
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Three killed after car strikes L.A. pedestrians, Democrats brace for Stephen Miller clashes, and Joe Biden targeted by protesters in Dublin
Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted objects at  former President Joe Biden outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said Wednesday.
Videos showed protesters, some waving Palestinian flags, chanting “Blood on your hands” and scuffling with police officers outside Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as he attended a ceremony honoring his son Hunter Biden, alongside former first lady Jill Biden . White liquid, believed to be milk, could also be seen flying through the air toward the group.
Hunter Biden was being honored by its traditional Hist debating society , which dates back to 1770. Previous recipients of the gold medal for outstanding contribution to public discourse include Irish musician Bob Geldof, South African Bishop Desmond Tutu , WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and the late Sen. Ted Kennedy.
During his acceptance speech, Hunter Biden discussed his addictions, family life and being in the public eye. “We are living in an age of bullies,” he said , adding that he had learned this from “my own scars.”
Shortly after the ceremony, a “protest took place in Trinity’s Front Square,” Catherine O’Mahony, a spokesperson for the college, said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday.
She said “the protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving,” and Irish police, known as the Gardaí, arrived at the scene. “The Biden family left without incident. The protest dispersed soon after,” she added.
Police said in a statement Wednesday that three adult males were arrested “in relation to a public order incident” at Trinity College Dublin. One man in his 50s “has since been charged and is due to appear before Court. The two other males have been released without charge.” The statement did not say what the man had been charged with.
Representatives for the elder Biden did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the incident.
Ireland has long had a historical solidarity with the Palestinian cause, with pro-Palestinian flags, murals and graffiti a common sight around the country.
Many in the country compare the current situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank with Ireland’s experience of British colonial rule and struggle for self-determination. Ireland was also the recent venue for American rapper Macklemore’s sold-out “Free Palestine Tour,” which opened in Dublin last month.
The Bidens, who have Irish heritage, also met with Ireland’s Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin.
“We reflected on his strong Irish roots and previous visits, appreciating his lifelong support for Ireland,” Martin said in a post on X, of his meeting with the former president.
During a 2023 visit to the country while he was president, Biden told the Irish parliament in an emotional address that he was “home.”
Biden’s great-great-grandfather Owen Finnegan left the Irish county of Louth for the United States in 1849, and he also has relatives from another side of his family in County Mayo, on Ireland’s west coast.
Earlier this week, Biden, 83, signaled he was scaling back public tours to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise Me, America,” as he continues his treatment for cancer.
“Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote Sunday in a lengthy post on X . “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”
Biden announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer months after he left office in January 2025 and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment.
He said his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment” and thanked the public for their prayers and well-wishes.
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.

articles.title_orig: Mama grizzly bear and her 3 cubs killed woman and daughter in Canada, DNA confirms: "Predatory behavior"
articles.title_zh: Mama grizzly bear and her 3 cubs killed woman and daughter in Canada, DNA confirms: "Predatory behavior"
articles.content_orig:
Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday.
DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
"Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare," Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing .
"That is to say, we don't know how it started, but we know how it ended."
The women's remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver.
Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother's remains first, then discovered Reed's remains in a bear cache, where bears store food.
Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.
The latest killings have shaken the Nuxalk Nation community, which is still recovering from last year's attack. Local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew, and police escorted children to school.
"This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack," said Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, the Nuxalk Nation's elected chief councilor.
He said community support services would remain available as long as needed.
Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be rehabilitated or relocated because they pose an extreme risk to public safety.
"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said.
There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks . The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.
In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.
A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

articles.title_orig: Asian shops targeted as Eswatini cracks down on illegal foreign businesses
articles.title_zh: Asian shops targeted as Eswatini cracks down on illegal foreign businesses
articles.content_orig:
Businesses owned by Asian nationals are being closed across Eswatini as the government cracks down on foreign-owned enterprises.
The crackdown follows Parliament's approval of the Citizen Economic Empowerment Act, which seeks to increase ownership and participation by emaSwati, as citizens in the kingdom are known.
The legislation follows complaints from local traders that foreign-owned businesses are encroaching on traditional retail markets, increasing competition and threatening livelihoods.
South Africa has witnessed more severe enforcement actions, including raids, arrests and the disruption of foreign-run informal businesses, while Kenya has also stepped up action against foreign traders.
Its implementation has sparked a heated debate in Parliament, with MPs divided over how quickly foreign businesses owners should be required to leave.
Mbabane East MP Welcome Dlamini told Parliament on Tuesday that officials from the trade ministry had already begun enforcing the law by closing Asian-owned shops.
Hhohho Regional MP Tanele Magagula called for immediate action, saying "Businesses owned by foreigners in the rural areas must be seized immediately."
But Dlamini questioned whether local entrepreneurs were ready to take over the businesses, arguing that foreigner should be given time tio train their successors.
"Why can't we give the Asians or foreigners at least three years before 'kicking them' out so that emaSwati can learn to run the businesses?" he asked.
Magagula rejected the suggestion, questioning why struggling local traders should have to wait while struggling economically.
"Why must we wait for three years while emaSwati suffer?" she asked.
Parliament subsequently agreed that foreign business owners should be given at least 12 months to leave.
However, unless the law is formally amended to reflect that timeline, the ministry could continue enforcing its provisions.
The closures follow  inspections launched by the trade ministry in August. Some businesses inspected in areas such as Mbabane were found to be fully compliant.
However, the inspections also raised concerns about working conditions an administrative practices at foreign-owned enterprises, including complaints by employees over days off, annual leave and overtime. At least one case remains under investigation.
Eswatini, a small landlocked kingdom in Southern Africa, faces significant economic hardship, with about 70% of its population living below the poverty line.
The government says the new law is intended to expand economic opportunities for citizens, amid concerns that poverty and hunger could fuel further political unrest.
The crackdown comes mid growing pressure on foreign-owned businesses elsewhere in the region, particularly in neighbouring South Africa, where anti-immigration campaigns have led to raids, arrests,looting and the disruption of foreign-run informal businesses.
On July 30, 2026, the March and March movement intensified its campaign against undocumented immigrants, giving them a deadline to leave. Another protest followed on September 30.
The campaigns have been accompanied by violence and attacks on foreign owned businesses.
Two Ghanaian and two Nigerian nationals reported killed amid the tensions.
Kenya has also stepped up enforcement against foreign traders, bring renewed attention to the treatment of foreign nationals and their businesses across the region.

articles.title_orig: ‘A restless and difficult night’ in the Baltics as NATO fighter jets fail to shoot down drone
articles.title_zh: ‘A restless and difficult night’ in the Baltics as NATO fighter jets fail to shoot down drone
articles.content_orig:
NATO fighter jets twice tried and failed to shoot down a drone over northern Lithuania overnight, as unidentified aerial objects triggered air-raid warnings across the Baltic states and prompted precautionary restrictions in Finland.
Three unmanned aircraft were initially detected operating in Belarusian airspace and moving north towards Latvia. Latvia’s armed forces subsequently reported that two additional aerial targets entered Latvian airspace from the direction of Belarus and later departed.
A fourth drone crossed from Belarus into Lithuania at around 1.20am local time (12.20am CET). It briefly entered Polish airspace before abruptly changing direction and returning to Lithuania.
NATO fighter jets tracked it as it travelled north towards the Latvian border, but two attempts to destroy it near Biržai, in northern Lithuania, were unsuccessful. One of the missiles fired by the fighter jets missed the drone and fell to the ground.
The drone subsequently crossed into Latvia, where fighters on NATO’s air policing mission could not get into position to shoot it down , allowing it to cross into Estonia and eventually into Russia.
The drone’s type, origin and whether it was carrying explosives remain unknown.
“We do not currently have confirmed information about the type of drone,” Rear Admiral Giedrius Premeneckas, chief of the Lithuanian Armed Forces Defence Staff, said at a press briefing early on Wednesday. It was not yet possible to determine whether the aircraft was Ukrainian or Russian, he added.
Ukraine had carried out a large-scale drone attack on Russia overnight and, according to Premeneckas, one possibility was that the aircraft had been diverted from its intended course by electronic warfare measures. But he stressed that this remained an assumption.
Overnight, authorities in all three Baltic states issued warnings urging residents to seek shelter as unidentified aerial objects approached or entered their airspace. Further north, Finland temporarily restricted aviation and maritime activity in the eastern Gulf of Finland, close to the Russian border.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda called the night “restless and difficult” in a Facebook post , warning that more incursions were possible.
“Unfortunately, as long as Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine continues, the incursion of combat drones into Lithuanian territory may happen again,” Nausėda said, calling on Lithuanians to “remain patient and understanding.”
The latest incident follows a series of drone incursions across the Baltic region in recent months.
In October, a suspected drone entered Lithuanian airspace and exploded in the country’s north , triggering air-raid alerts and prompting NATO fighter jets to scramble. In September, NATO aircraft also shot down a drone over Lithuania , while an earlier incident in May saw a Romanian NATO fighter jet destroy a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia after it entered from Russia. Latvia has also reported repeated incursions, including a drone that struck an oil storage facility in May.
In Lithuania, the drone activity on Tuesday night coincided with a separate wave of suspected meteorological balloons, further complicating the overnight response.
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre, described the night as “the most unsettled in the country’s history,” citing both the drone incidents and the balloons.
He also noted that Belarusian authorities had informed Lithuania about objects detected on their side of the border that could potentially be moving towards Lithuanian airspace.
“This is a welcome development. Such cases have been rare recently,” he said, referring to the information passed on by Belarus.
Around 10 balloon-related radar sightings were recorded, disrupting airport operations. Aircraft were allowed to depart, but landing operations were restricted, affecting three flights and forcing around 470 passengers to change their plans, Vitkauskas said.
He also warned against disinformation circulating online suggesting Lithuania was allowing Ukrainian drones to use its airspace to attack Russia.
“That is an absolute lie,” he said, urging residents to follow official emergency instructions and not to ignore alerts sent to their phones.
The National Security Commission was also due to discuss access to public shelters on Wednesday, with Vitkauskas acknowledging that reaching shelters during a night-time emergency can be difficult. Residents without access to a shelter were advised to follow the two-wall principle, stay away from windows and seek refuge in a basement where possible.
“The events of last night will be thoroughly investigated,” Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in a Facebook post.

articles.title_orig: What 400 years of hot IPOs say about buying Anthropic on day one: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: What 400 years of hot IPOs say about buying Anthropic on day one: Chart of the Day

Oops, something went wrong
Anthropic's roadshow is selling the future of AI. Four centuries of hot IPOs say the first trade is rarely the best one.
The AI lab is asking for as much as $1.4 trillion at the top of its $70-to-$78 range, counting every possible share . Trading could start as soon as next week. Rival OpenAI ( OPAI.PRV ) may not be far behind: OpenAI president Greg Brockman said last week the company could be ready to go public next year.
History has a warning for anyone planning to buy on the first day . The world's first IPO, the Dutch East India Company, began trading in 1602. Its stock took about three decades to double .
This year brought two fresh reminders. SpaceX ( SPCX ) opened at $150 in June, $15 above its IPO price, and soared about 40% in its first week. By August, it was in a nearly 30% hole. Five months later, SpaceX is still below its first trade.
Cerebras ( CBRS ) had it worse. The AI chipmaker opened at nearly double its $185 IPO price in May. Its first close is still its best, and the stock now trades at about half what IPO buyers paid.
Anthropic's growth is anything but typical. Revenue in the first nine months of the year was 13 times what it was a year earlier. But investors are being asked to pay up for it. At $78 a share, Anthropic would trade at about 29 times its sales over the past year, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
University of Florida professor Jay Ritter tracked more than 4,000 IPOs of companies with at least $100 million in sales since 1980. Those priced at 20 to 40 times sales gained about 3% on average over three years from their first close. The cheapest gained about 41%.
There's a bright spot for Anthropic. IPOs of the biggest companies, those with more than $1 billion in sales, did about as well as the market.
A big first-day pop would make the math worse. A jump of about 40% would push Anthropic past 40 times sales, where IPOs lost nearly half their value over three years.
That pop goes to whoever buys at the IPO offering price , usually big Wall Street firms and their wealthy clients. It has averaged nearly 20% since 1975, Ritter's data shows, and everyone buying after the open pays for it. This time, Anthropic is setting aside up to a fifth of its shares for retail brokers including Schwab, Fidelity, and Robinhood.
Other companies are racing to sell stock before the deal, competing for the same investors' dollars. "The Anthropic IPO is almost becoming this magnet where everybody's trying to raise liquidity in front of them," Peachtree Creek Investments founder Conor Sen said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang in November.
Dan Niles of Niles Investment Management recalled the dot-com bust, when the S&P 500 staged seven rallies on the way down, to Yahoo Finance on Monday.
"You'd be like, wow, it's a great time to invest. Except you would have lost 49% of your money because that's the tech bubble."

articles.title_zh: Consumers are turning to cheaper brands like it's 2021 as inflation pinches

The verdict is in, or nearly there. After Tuesday's hotter-than-expected inflation numbers , the Fed is most likely going to raise interest rates at its policy meeting next month.
On top of that, investors are now worried about a much more hawkish Fed in 2027.
Pricing pressures were so strong across essentials like food, rent, and medical care that there's renewed chatter the Fed might impose a jumbo hike of 50 basis points.
The expectations have clearly changed.
Higher costs are showing up in other places too. Like in data about how Americans are spending their money . According to a new analysis by the Bank of America Institute, consumers are "trading down" to cheaper brands at the highest levels since the height of the pandemic.
The data reveals that consumers are increasingly value-conscious. People are buying store brands over name brands, going to cheaper retailers instead of department stores, and eating fast food in place of sit-down restaurants.
"While households continue to spend, they are increasingly seeking discounts as concerns about higher prices persist," wrote Taylor Bowley, an economist at the Bank of America Institute. With a ton of deposit accounts, credit cards, and debit cards, the bank is uniquely positioned to track spending across a wide swath of demographics.
The analysis showed consumers appear increasingly focused on value, shifting spending to value-tier merchants at 2021 levels. Millennials — faced with the cost of raising families, high housing, auto, and childcare costs — are leading the shift toward value-oriented shopping, the report found.
That change is most pronounced in apparel and grocery spending, suggesting that the hunt for bargains isn't limited to discretionary purchases but now extends to everyday household spending.
"While consumers can delay apparel purchases, trading down on groceries is notable because it suggests Millennials are looking for savings even in areas where spending is harder to avoid, like food," the report said.

articles.title_orig: Italy evacuates hundreds of schools after receiving email bomb threats
articles.title_zh: Italy evacuates hundreds of schools after receiving email bomb threats
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of schools were evacuated in Italy on Wednesday after bomb threats were sent via email, police told CNN, becoming the latest in a series of threats and cyberattacks targeting infrastructure across Europe.
Schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland also received emails Wednesday, although police warned these were likely hoaxes and education facilities were not evacuated.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in a statement that there was currently no indication that a “concrete danger exists.”
“The exact number of schools is undetermined, as the emails were sent to hundreds of them and then each school decides when to evacuate following the advice of the local police branch,” the spokesperson for the Italian police said.
Authorities are investigating the source of the email, the spokesperson said, declining to confirm the email address the communication came from.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara told Italian TV that about 300 schools across Italy had received the threats, but downplayed them as related to cyber attacks and not a “genuine risk.”
In central Rome, dozens of kindergarten and primary school children enjoyed a day off as the Quirinio Visconti primary school was evacuated. Their parents were notified to pick them up, a teacher told CNN.
Meloni said the government was “following very closely” reports of the threats directed at schools, saying the incidents appeared aimed at “generating alarm and concern.”
The Italian prime minister said the government was “doing everything necessary to ensure the safety of citizens.”
In Northern Ireland, more than 300 schools received a threatening email, police said Wednesday, adding that the message originated outside the United Kingdom and was being treated as a hoax.
“Our enquiries are ongoing, however, at this stage we consider risk to the public as low,” Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally said in a statement.
The Education Authority said the message sent to “a large number of schools” in Northern Ireland resembled a hoax sent to schools last month and that it was unaware of any evidence of a “credible” threat.
Police in the Republic of Ireland said a generic communication had been sent to “a number of educational establishments” Wednesday. Police assessed the threat as “not credible” and said they were not advising any evacuations.
Meanwhile, Police Scotland said “threatening messages” were sent to schools. The force said the messages were being treated as hoaxes and advised schools that the emails alone did not warrant evacuation.
Wednesday’s incident is the latest in a series targeting infrastructure and organizations across Europe. Last week, a string of hoax bomb threats disrupted dozens of flights and media organizations across the continent.
This story has been updated with developments.
CNN’s Niamh Kennedy contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Savvy entrepreneurs are driving a surge in data-center RV parks
articles.title_zh: Savvy entrepreneurs are driving a surge in data-center RV parks
articles.content_orig:
Seventy Amazon packages were piled up at an RV park near Cedar Rapids, Iowa.
They weren't for the tourists passing through to attend an antique show or see the nearby historic German villages, says Jamie Wolter, the manager of Amana RV Park & Event Center. They're for the hundreds of data center workers now living at the park.
Typically, the 450-campsite park hosts up to 60 long-term campers, but now that Google and QTS are both building data centers in the area, workers have come from as far away as Oregon and Washington. Some bring spouses and children they homeschool. Staff who used to field complaints about missing fire rings now have to decide whether to ask someone who's behind on rent to move their home.
"It's like you're a landlord now, and you never used to be," Wolter says.
Still, she credits the data center workers with helping mitigate a decline in RV tourists due to gas prices. "Without these long-term guests, it would have been terrible."
As construction workers crisscross the country for high-paying data center jobs , some are putting their per diem toward an RV. While working on one of the biggest infrastructure buildouts in US history, they could be at a site anywhere from a few months to a few years, often in places where hotels and short-term rentals are scarce or expensive. If they find a spot in packed campsites, a travel trailer can stretch their housing allowance further, shorten their commute , and make room for family and pets — all while "chasing that data center money" . It can also go with them to the next job when construction ends .
The trend is a much-needed boost for the RV industry, which has tumbled from its pandemic high . US wholesale RV shipments fell 13.7% through September compared with the same period last year; sales to data center workers are helping some dealers weather the slump. Meanwhile, campgrounds built for tourists are filling up with data center workers — and their operators are learning what it means to be flooded with long-term tenants.
At ATC RV Center in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, data center workers helped keep unit sales roughly flat from a year earlier. "Without them, it would have been really slow for us," manager Joel Philipp says.
Because RVs are largely a leisure purchase, sales are especially exposed when households cut back. "It's usually the first into a recession and the last out," he says of the industry. "You don't need it, you want it."
His dealership used geofencing to target ads to people using their phones around data center construction sites . The idea was to reach workers interested in RVs on their breaks, when they browse Facebook or ESPN on their phones — and it worked. A number of those people turned up to buy RVs, he says.
In Louisiana, Bayou Outdoor Supercenter offers workers on Meta's Hyperion projec t a calculator that compares the cost of staying in a hotel with the cost of buying an RV they can take to their next job.
At Clear Creek RVs in Abilene, marketing director Shannon Calkins estimates about half the dealership's business now comes from data center workers. Before the buildout, workers buying RVs for housing, including people on pipeline and solar projects, accounted for about 15% to 20% of its business. Calkins credits new customers with helping Clear Creek continue to grow in a difficult market.
Most data center buyers opt for smaller, cheaper travel trailers, Calkins says. Her finance team has seen per diems ranging from about $100 to $300 a day. A smaller trailer can cost around $20,000, and depending on the loan, payments can come in at $400 a month or less. A $400 trailer paired with a $600 campsite would put the cost at $1,000 a month before electricity, insurance, or food.
Calkins says some buyers have limited credit histories, which can make loans harder to get and more expensive when they do qualify. But a worker who would otherwise spend that money on hotel rooms can put some of it toward a trailer they'll still own when the job is over. In Cedar Rapids, Philipp did see some demand for larger fifth-wheel RVs, which he says could run $60,000 to $70,000, but those typically came from coworkers looking for bunkhouse models they could share or tradespeople bringing their families.
At Abilene RV Park in Texas, all the weekly and monthly spaces and long-term cabins were full when I spoke with manager Debbie Coffey. Data center workers make up most of her long-term guests, and she says there's continually a waitlist of 20 to 30 people.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Coffey spends so much time handling deliveries that she feels "like a mail lady about half the day every day." There's more work keeping up the showers, restrooms, and laundry room, too. The park recently increased its monthly rate by $50, to $600 plus electricity, to help cover higher property taxes and upkeep costs.
She keeps about five of the park's 66 spaces open for people passing through, the guests she's counting on to come back when data center construction winds down.
Near Meta's sprawling data center campus in Richland Parish, Louisiana, Corporate Mobile Housing's Dunn Village provides construction workers with rooms in mobile homes as well as 170 spaces for them to bring their own RVs. Heather Kleinpeter, the company's director of strategic growth, says data centers have given a new life to a business whose owners had been considering retirement. Founded after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 to house workers pumping water out of New Orleans, the business later pivoted to accommodating oil and gas workers. Prior to Meta's Louisiana data center announcement in late 2024, Corporate Mobile Housing provided 300 beds. It's now at 1,500, and Kleinpeter expects that number to double next year.
Two of Kleinpeter's sons work in data centers and have both lived in modular housing at Dunn Village. In her parks and around Richland Parish, she sees all kinds of workers living in RVs, from younger ones who don't need much space to retirees picking up work again to people traveling with kids or dogs. That means campers with little fences, swings, and kids' bikes out front. At some parks, food trucks have set up shop to sell breakfast.
"People are just taking advantage of the opportunity on every level," she says.
The opportunity comes with an end date. Meta says its expanded Richland Parish campus will support more than 7,500 jobs at peak construction and 1,000 once it's operating. When data construction projects finish, the traveling crews will need another job — and somewhere else to park their RVs.
Kleinpeter says Corporate Mobile Housing is planning five to seven years out. Afterward, the company could move some of the modular homes to another job or find a new use for land it has already equipped with water, sewer, and electricity. It depends on what the parish looks like then.
"It's going to be a collective like, 'What does the municipality want?'" Kleinpeter says.
Future data center projects also face a tougher political climate. In this month's midterms , Texas elected Gina Hinojosa, who backs a statewide moratorium on new data center approvals, as governor. Texas accounts for about one in five US data center buildings that are planned or under construction, according to industry tracker Cleanview . Michigan backed Abdul El-Sayed, who has called for a pause on new developments, for the Senate. Voters in several towns across the country also approved measures to restrict or ban new data centers .
Around Abilene, Calkins has watched new RV parks pop up in fields, some little more than crushed gravel and utility hookups. Some of these parks have plenty of space, she says, even while established parks are turning away monthly renters. When the work dries up, she figures the crews will hitch up their trailers and take them to the next job.
It's the parks they leave behind that she thinks will sell for "pennies on the dollar."

articles.title_orig: Pope Returns to Peru, Where Evangelicals Challenge Catholic Dominance
articles.title_zh: Pope Returns to Peru, Where Evangelicals Challenge Catholic Dominance
articles.content_orig:
Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories will likely be front of mind among the public as they welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday — a trip that will include visits to Lima, Cusco, Chiclayo and several other cities.
A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis.
“I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic.
Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator.
“He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop.
Pope! Amigo! Peruvians remember the young American priest who became pope
Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis.
“He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added.
Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths , according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus.
In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants.
Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023.
“We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN.
Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country.
“I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region.
The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions.
Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.
First American pope marks July 4 on migrant island with plea for ‘compassion and generosity’
“The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled.
Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén.
“His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN.
Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society.
Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s.
At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered.
Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures.
Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo.
His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave.
Pope Leo presides at biggest Mass of his papacy in Buenos Aires, drawing 2.5 million crowd
In the past, the election of an American pope was considered impossible, given that the College of Cardinals did not wish to associate the papacy with the dominant political and cultural power. However, the cardinals who voted for Cardinal Robert Prevost in the 2025 conclave did not see him simply as a candidate from the United States. His experience in Peru garnered broad consensus among the cardinals, who chose a bishop with roots in Latin America — someone who speaks Spanish fluently and is attuned to the concerns of the people of that continent.
The pope’s visit to Peru is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who is a Peruvian citizen and who knows the country in depth.
Reverend John Lydon, a priest and member of the same Augustinian religious order to which the pope belongs, and who lived and worked with Prevost for a decade, told CNN: “I believe his dedication to the poor and his defense of human rights will continue to define his visit.”

articles.title_orig: Rafael Unveils Super Ice Cruise Missile with 1,000-lb Warhead
articles.title_zh: Rafael Unveils Super Ice Cruise Missile with 1,000-lb Warhead
articles.content_orig:
Rafael Advanced Defense Systems on Tuesday unveiled its new "Super Ice" cruise missile which was designed to continue to surprise various enemies in the future who may have learned many of Israel's tactics in recent years.
Super Ice is the next generation of the Icebreaker cruise missile, launched in 2021-2022, which includes a warhead which is four times the size of the earlier generation, but has managed to reach a faster speed and longer range.
With a 1,000 pound warhead compared to the Icebreaker's 250 pound warhead, Super Ice is far more destructive.
In addition, despite the weight of the warhead, Super Ice can be fired off of all of Israel's major aircraft, F-35, F-16, and F-15.
In contrast, there are some even heavier weapons, which can only be fired from the F-15 , an older aircraft lacking stealth capabilities.
Rafael sources declined to disclose the new extended range of Super Ice, but the Icebreaker missile had a 300 kilometer plus range, which means the new product certainly exceeds that.
Likewise, Rafael sources declined to reveal the new higher speed which Super Ice can achieve, but Icebreaker was able to reach at least Mach 0.8-0.9, such that the new model can certainly outperform those speeds.
Generally, the advantage of a cruise missile like Super Ice, as with Icebreaker, is to serve as a lightweight, low altitude, autonomous weapon system which can surprise strategic and well-guarded enemy targets, giving them a very short time warning period before they are struck (which is insufficient warning to defend).
Featuring the powerful 1,000-pound warhead (MK83 compatible), Super Ice also "supports multiple launch platforms across air, land, and sea, providing maximum operational flexibility."
"The missile incorporates advanced capabilities, including robust autonomous navigation, low-altitude terrain-following flight, all-weather operation and high-precision engagement of diverse targets. Its advanced electro-optical guidance system employs high-accuracy image-matching technology," said Rafael.
Senior Vice President and Head of Rafael's Air Systems Division Gad Geva said, "SUPER ICE™ was developed for integration across a wide range of aerial platforms without requiring significant modifications to the platforms themselves."
"The missile's multi-domain design also enables launch from air, sea, or ground-based launchers. Together, SUPER ICE™ and ICE BREAKER™ provide an operationally effective and cost-efficient solution, allowing customers to select the appropriate weapon system for each target. Significant savings in mission-planning requirements and life-cycle costs further enhance the family's value," said Geva.
Rafael sources did not designate Super Ice as being developed to handle a specific existing threat which prior Israeli weaponry had not succeeded in coping with.
For example, in addition to Icebreaker and Super Ice, Rafael produces the Blue Sparrow ballistic missile, which according to foreign sources has been used multiple times to strike strategic Iranian targets in past years.
Some have speculated that Rafael's ROCKS or Golden Horizon weapons may have also been used against Iran.
Rather, Super Ice is designed to jump past even future defense systems which Iran and other adversaries might try to develop.
Interestingly, Super Ice is usable in the naval context, and Israel has spoken more publicly of late about possible conflict with Turkey's navy , which is more advanced than other Israeli adversaries.
A next generation missile like Super Ice will also sell well with European countries seeking weapons which can deter Russian expansionism, and could also sell well with countries in Asia wanting to deter China.
While Ice Breaker already incorporated advanced AI, electro-optical systems, and anti-jamming systems, it is understood that those and other systems in Super Ice are even more advanced.
While unveiled on Tuesday, the missile is expected to be operational more in the timeframe of early 2027.

articles.title_orig: Oil Rebounds After Two-Day Drop on U.S.-Iran Conflict Uncertainty
articles.title_zh: Oil Rebounds After Two-Day Drop on U.S.-Iran Conflict Uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
International oil benchmark Brent crude briefly fell below $90 a barrel for the first time since August on Tuesday as comments from U.S. President Donald Trump fueled hopes for an end to Washington's nearly nine-month conflict with Iran.
Brent, the price gauge for around 80% of global crude, settled down 1.17% at $91.49 a barrel. At its session low, the international benchmark slid to $89.16. U.S. WTI crude fell 0.93% to settle at $86.04 a barrel.
Trump said on Monday that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon" and that Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington.
"We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," he said at the White House following a meeting with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. "Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump told reporters.
Trump also said in a Truth Social post that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait would "prefer the status quo," namely maintaining a naval blockade against Iran and preventing the country from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.
Crude oil prices have been highly volatile this year, proving sensitive to any perceived shift in direction in the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran.
Brent crude started the year around $60 a barrel before soaring as high as $130 a barrel as military strikes escalated in March and April. Prices retreated in June and July before climbing back to those levels as the conflict increasingly appeared entrenched.
Crude oil flows through the key Strait of Hormuz waterway have largely recovered . But consumers have suffered from resulting volatility in energy markets, as wider global conflicts — including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the Russia-Ukraine war — exacerbate a shortage of refining capacity, sending prices of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel soaring.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both acknowledged that public disapproval of the Iran war and high energy prices played a role in the Republicans' punishing result in the U.S. midterms last week .
While officials on both sides have continued to trade hostile words, particularly as they debate control of the Strait of Hormuz , the U.S. had largely held back on military strikes since September, with Trump saying in early October they would not resume until after the midterms.
The U.S. carried out what Trump called "minor strikes" on Iran after reports that two missiles struck Qeshm Island, located near the Strait of Hormuz off the country's southern coast.
Analysts were divided on how the U.S. administration would approach the Iran conflict after the Democrats' resounding midterm victories, with some viewing escalation as a strong possibility despite the initial market reaction suggesting hopes of a deal.
"The market has continued to unwind some of the geopolitical risk premium built into prices in recent weeks as expectations grow that the conflict between the US and Iran could move towards de-escalation," ING strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a note Tuesday.
"Signs that regional oil flows are recovering have added to the downward pressure... Reports that Iran may be softening its position on control of the Strait of Hormuz have also reduced concerns over a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most important oil transit routes."
"For now, the return of more Gulf barrels and the prospect of easing tensions are taking some of the geopolitical premium out of crude. However, with regional negotiations still uncertain and infrastructure risks persisting, we expect oil prices to remain sensitive to developments in the Middle East."
Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman of energy consultancy FGE, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Tuesday that, despite market moves, he still did not see any prospects of a peace deal between the U.S. and Iran.
"The difference between the two sides is so wide, it cannot be bridged. Most importantly, the U.S. wants all the nuclear material, enriched material, to be transferred out of Iran, and there is no way that the Iranian regime would agree to this, and there is no way the Iranian regime would agree to let the Strait of Hormuz be open for a free flow of oil the way it was before the war," Fesharaki said.
"So, with these two in between, I just can't see a deal being made.
"Trump has to decide. Either he says, 'I declare victory and walk away,' or he goes to war. If he goes to war, he's got only a window of two weeks from today for himself and for [Israeli Prime Minister] Netanyahu, or there will be no war at all on a long-term basis," Fesharaki added.
Netanyahu's political party failed to win a majority in Israel's election last month, with rival Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of the Israel Defense Forces, officially tasked with forming a government on Sunday.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this story.
Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the session low for Brent crude.

articles.title_orig: Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
articles.title_zh: Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
articles.content_orig:
On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.
Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux . It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.
A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available.
Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution.
The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.
If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.
You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system .
Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update.
Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability.
Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component.
XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data.
A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.
Google only says that it is “aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” It has not named the attackers, the targets, the delivery method, or what the exploit can do.

The Kremlin is attempting to center the ongoing US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi around significant changes to the European security architecture — an effort to revive its 2021 ultimatums to the United States and NATO about rolling back NATO’s presence in Europe. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed on November 10 that it is “absolutely reasonable” to first negotiate the future of the European security architecture and only then move to resolving the war in Ukraine.[1] An unspecified source in the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi similarly claimed on November 10 that the settlement of the war in Ukraine is “only one point” in a larger discussion on security architecture and is “subordinated” to the main goal of reshaping Europe’s “comprehensive” and “indivisible” security architecture.[2] Russian statements about the European security architecture refer to Russia’s December 2021 demands that NATO halt new weapons and military personnel deployments to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997, essentially giving Russia a veto on NATO policy and restricting states’ sovereign choices to join NATO.[3] The Kremlin recently renewed its original 2021 demands of NATO, contradicting Former Senior Advisor to the US President Jared Kushner’s statements in recent days that each country must retain its sovereignty and authority over its security and alliances following peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and that NATO will remain central to European collective defense.[4]
The Kremlin has repeatedly tried to justify its war against Ukraine by falsely claiming that the possibility of NATO expansion to include Ukraine threatened Russian security. The Kremlin has long alleged that NATO expansion was one of the “root causes” of the war that peace talks must resolve.[5] Neither NATO nor Ukraine, in fact, took any meaningful action towards bringing Ukraine into NATO between 2008 and 2022, however.[6] NATO has never presented a threat to Russian security, but Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022 to break NATO and Western unity, as ISW has long assessed.[7] The Kremlin’s long-running cognitive warfare campaign falsely blaming NATO and Ukraine for threatening Russian sovereignty aims to justify Russian efforts to reassert control over former Soviet states and does not reflect a genuine Russian concern for its security.
US, Ukrainian, and European officials publicly agreed on the need for credible post-war security guarantees for Ukraine and the involvement of European officials in future multilateral negotiations to end the war in Ukraine — conditions that the Kremlin has repeatedly and explicitly rejected. US, Ukrainian, and European officials held trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi wherein they agreed on the need for credible security guarantees for Ukraine and the involvement of European officials in future multilateral negotiations to end the war.[8] US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, and Kushner emphasized on November 9 and 10 that a lasting settlement to the war requires durable post-war security guarantees for Ukraine, future involvement of European officials in peace negotiations, and direct engagement between Russia and European officials on broader geopolitical security arrangements.[9] Several Western media outlets reported on November 9 and 10 that US officials asked the Kremlin if it would accept NATO-style Article 4 and Article 5 security guarantees for Ukraine from the United States and NATO that would allow Ukraine to request consultations with NATO states when Ukraine’s territorial integrity is under threat and to receive assistance from the alliance in the event of a future attack.[10]
Russian officials have repeatedly rejected the idea of Western security guarantees for Ukraine since 2025 and the possibility of European officials having a seat at the negotiating table so long as the European position falls short of fully embracing Russia’s maximalist demands.[11] Lavrov claimed on November 10 that US meetings with European representatives in Abu Dhabi are not a “promising approach” to negotiations.[12] Russian State Duma Deputy Alexander Asafov stated on November 10 that Russia’s expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks are “quite modest” and claimed that European participation in the talks could “paralyze” negotiations before they even begin.[13] These statements are consistent with Moscow’s explicit rejections in previous weeks of European participation in negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and go against US, Ukrainian, and European statements in favor of including European officials in future peace talks.[14]
Reported proposals to redraw the administrative borders of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts to allow Russia to claim that it seized all of the Donbas region and compel Russia to accept a deal to end the war neglect Moscow’s wider territorial aims in Ukraine that go far beyond these two oblasts. The Economist reported on November 9 that US negotiators recently proposed that Ukraine change the administrative borders of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts as part of a territorial agreement between Russia and Ukraine such that Russia could claim full control of the two regions without Ukraine surrendering the remaining territory of Donbas that it currently holds.[15] The reported proposal suggests that the new oblast borders would correspond to the territory in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts that Russian forces have seized, although it is unclear what legal status the Ukrainian-controlled territory in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts would have. Russian President Vladimir Putin has demonstrated, however, that his territorial ambitions in Ukraine go far beyond Donbas.[16] Russia illegally annexed Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhia oblasts in September 2022, and the Kremlin has long conditioned Russian society to expect Russia’s illegal annexation of these parts of Ukraine to be permanent.[17] Russian officials also regularly claim that “Novorossiya” — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine — is an integral part of Russia.[18] Novorossiya notably includes not only occupied Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed, but also the Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.[19]
Putin and the Russian military command have created a false reality based on exaggerated claims of sweeping advances across the frontline such that the Kremlin would likely try to exploit any discussion of redrawing administrative borders based on the frontline to serve Russia’s interest. Senior Russian military and political officials regularly make blatantly false claims of Russian advances on the frontline, often as far as tens of kilometers from the observed frontline.[20] Putin notably claimed on September 2 that Russian forces had seized Svyatohirsk (14 kilometers northwest of Lyman), despite Ukrainian counterattacks having pushed the frontline over 20 kilometers east of the settlement.[21] A leaked Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) map from April 2026 also demonstrated that the Russian military command has a severely distorted view of the frontline, with claims of Russian advances in western Zaporizhia Oblast far beyond even the furthest claims from Russian milbloggers at that time.[22] The Russian MoD has also made several false claims in recent months about the encirclement of Ukrainian forces in northern Kharkiv Oblast and Dobropillya, Donetsk Oblast, despite providing no evidence to support the claims.[23] These exaggerations are a part of a broader cognitive warfare effort that aims to convince the West to force Ukraine to capitulate to Russia’s demands.[24] Such a vast disconnect between the true battlefield realities and Russian official claims about the frontline would complicate any attempt to redraw the administrative boundaries of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts and would risk Moscow claiming it holds more territor
